strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting: using conditional mean and covariance information to improve diffusion/flow-based forecasting under non-stationarity and distribution shift.

The proposed conditional whitening idea is intuitive and potentially broadly applicable, since it can wrap several existing diffusion and flow matching forecasters rather than requiring an entirely new generative backbone.

The empirical setup includes multiple real-world datasets and several recent generative baselines, and the reported ETTh1 results show substantial improvements for several models on CRPS, ProbCorr, and Conditional FID.
The paper makes a useful attempt to connect the method design to KL-divergence considerations and to motivate covariance/eigenvalue regularization in the estimator.
weaknesses: The manuscript is incomplete as submitted: it repeatedly refers to Appendix A-E, Theorem 2, algorithms, ablations, hyperparameters, metric definitions, and Tables 3-8, but these are not present in the provided PDF. This severely limits verifiability and reproducibility.

The theoretical contribution is not sufficiently convincing from the main text alone. Theorem 1 gives a sufficient condition for reducing KL to a fitted Gaussian, but the proof is absent, the condition depends on unknown true moments, and the link from reduced terminal KL to better learned generative samples is asserted rather than rigorously established for the proposed trained models.

There is a mismatch between the theory and implementation: the theorem concerns the true full conditional covariance, while the method estimates a per-time sliding-window covariance. The consequences of ignoring cross-time covariance and using a surrogate covariance target are not theoretically justified.

The experimental evidence is only partially visible. Only one detailed results table appears in the manuscript, while most claimed win rates and conclusions rely on missing tables. This makes it impossible to independently assess consistency across datasets, metrics, and model families.

The evaluation does not clearly separate gains from the proposed generative whitening from gains due to adding a powerful forecasting model, JMCE. Stronger ablations are needed, such as mean-only, diagonal variance-only, full covariance, oracle statistics, alternative covariance estimators, and comparisons under matched parameter/training budgets.

Computational cost and scalability are under-discussed. Estimating and regularizing covariance matrices, especially for high-dimensional datasets such as Solar Energy with 137 variables, may be expensive, yet runtime, memory, and sampling/training overhead are not reported in the visible manuscript.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence shown, especially regarding distribution-shift mitigation and improved inter-variable dependency modeling. The paper provides qualitative plots and aggregate win rates, but no dedicated shift protocol or rigorous dependency evaluation is visible.

Reproducibility is weak in the provided version: implementation details, model configurations, algorithms, hyperparameter choices beyond a few constants, and code availability are missing or deferred to absent appendices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting under non-stationarity, heteroscedasticity, inter-variable dependence, and distribution shift.
The high-level idea of using conditional mean and covariance estimates to transform or parameterize the generative process is intuitive and relevant to diffusion/flow forecasting models.
The method is modular in principle: the proposed CW-Diff/CW-Flow wrapper can be applied to several existing generative forecasting models rather than only one architecture.

The experimental setup, as described, considers multiple real-world datasets and several recent diffusion/flow baselines, and reports probabilistic metrics such as CRPS, QICE, correlation-based scores, and conditional FID.
weaknesses: The submitted manuscript is incomplete: it repeatedly refers to Appendix A-E for key limitations, proofs, algorithms, metrics, ablations, hyperparameters, dataset details, and additional results, but these appendices are not present in the provided PDF. Tables 3-6 and Tables 7-8 are also referenced but absent. This is a major reproducibility and evaluation problem.

The theoretical contribution is weakly connected to the actual modeling claims. Theorem 1 gives a sufficient condition for reducing KL to a fitted Gaussian terminal distribution, but this condition is largely an accuracy/eigenvalue requirement on the estimators and does not convincingly imply better learned generative forecasts after finite-sample training, score approximation, numerical sampling, or model misspecification.

The claimed novelty is limited. Whitening or standardizing data using conditional mean/variance/covariance estimates is a natural extension of prior-informed diffusion methods such as CARD, TMDM, and NsDiff. The paper does not clearly establish why this is a substantial conceptual advance rather than a covariance-aware preprocessing/prior module.

The covariance treatment appears incomplete for multivariate time series: the method estimates per-time-step sliding-window feature covariance, but does not model the full cross-time covariance structure. This undercuts claims about capturing temporal dependence and the full conditional covariance of future trajectories.

The evaluation evidence in the main paper is insufficient. Only one detailed result table is visible, despite claims over five datasets and many metrics. The win-rate summary is not enough to assess effect sizes, failure cases, statistical significance, or whether improvements are consistent across models and datasets.

Important baselines and controls are missing or not visible: simple normalization/whitening baselines, mean-only and diagonal-variance variants, alternative covariance estimators, RevIN-style preprocessing, and comparisons to strong non-generative probabilistic forecasting methods would be necessary to isolate the value of the proposed JMCE/CW design.

The method introduces substantial extra machinery, including training JMCE and estimating covariance matrices, but the paper does not adequately report computational cost, memory overhead, stability, or scaling behavior, especially for high-dimensional datasets such as Solar Energy.

The paper makes broad claims about mitigating distribution shift, but the evidence shown is mostly qualitative and based on standard train/test splits. There is no convincing stress test under controlled shifts, out-of-distribution regimes, or changing covariance structures.

Several design choices are under-justified, including sliding-window size, lambda_min, eigenvalue penalty weight, Cholesky/eigendecomposition choices, and how JMCE hyperparameters are tuned without leaking evaluation information.
Writing and presentation are uneven, with typos and imprecise claims. More importantly, central claims are stated more strongly than the provided theory and visible experiments support.

strengths: Clear and useful idea: conditionally whitening future trajectories with learned mean and covariance priors is a natural, modular way to make diffusion and flow models handle non-stationarity, heteroscedasticity, and cross-variable dependence better.

The method is broadly applicable: the paper demonstrates integration with multiple diffusion models and a flow-matching model, which supports the claim that CW-Gen is a framework rather than a single architecture.
Empirical results are encouraging across five real-world datasets and several probabilistic forecasting metrics, with repeated runs and reported standard deviations.
The paper makes a good attempt to connect the design to theory via KL reduction conditions and uses this analysis to motivate the JMCE objective.
The exposition is mostly readable, with a coherent progression from theory to estimator design to CW-Diff/CW-Flow implementations.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are only indirectly connected to the practical method. Theorem 1 concerns reducing KL to a Gaussian with true conditional mean/covariance, while the implemented JMCE estimates sliding-window covariance rather than the full conditional covariance of the future trajectory, leaving a substantial theory-practice gap.

The sample-quality claim relies on KL to a terminal Gaussian as a proxy; the paper does not fully establish that the proposed terminal replacement improves the learned reverse process under realistic score-estimation error or finite-sample training.

The flow-matching extension is empirically plausible but less theoretically supported than CW-Diff; the paper mainly transfers the intuition rather than providing an equally strong analysis for CW-Flow.

The experimental section is promising but somewhat incomplete in the visible manuscript: many claimed ablations, dataset details, hyperparameters, and additional tables are deferred to appendices that are not included here, limiting reproducibility and independent assessment.

The comparison mostly evaluates Raw versus CW variants of the same models. This is useful for isolating the contribution, but the paper would be stronger with clearer comparison to best tuned prior-informed methods, calibration diagnostics, runtime/memory overhead, and statistical significance tests.
Computational cost and scalability are under-discussed, especially for estimating and using covariance matrices in high-dimensional settings such as Solar Energy with 137 variables.

Some claims are stronger than the presented evidence, particularly around mitigating distribution shift and capturing inter-variable correlations; these would benefit from controlled shift experiments and more direct correlation/covariance evaluation.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and broadly applicable idea: use learned conditional mean and covariance estimates to whiten future time-series targets before training diffusion or flow-matching forecasters, then invert or modify the terminal distribution at sampling time.

The method is integrated with several recent generative forecasting models, including both diffusion and flow-matching variants, which supports the claim that CW-Gen is a wrapper-style framework rather than a single architecture.

The empirical tables cover five public datasets, six base generative models, multiple probabilistic metrics, and repeated runs with standard deviations. The reported gains are often large, especially for CRPS, ProbCorr, and conditional FID.
The paper includes useful ablations on JMCE eigenvalue regularization, backbone choice, mean vs variance/covariance components, sliding-window length, and an end-to-end training variant.
The exposition is generally understandable, and the algorithms in the appendix make the training and sampling procedures relatively clear.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is limited and only loosely connected to the implemented method. Theorem 1 gives a sufficient condition for KL improvement under an estimated full conditional Gaussian, but the actual method estimates a per-time sliding-window covariance, not the full conditional covariance over the future trajectory. This weakens the claimed theoretical justification.

The KL condition is somewhat tautological: if the estimated Gaussian is closer in mean/covariance to the conditional distribution and has controlled eigenvalues, it improves over the standard normal. It does not provide a finite-sample guarantee that JMCE will satisfy the condition, nor does it directly bound forecasting performance for the trained neural generative model.

The evaluation is not fully convincing as a top-tier contribution. Most comparisons are Raw model vs the same model with an additional trained JMCE prior, so gains may partly reflect added capacity, extra supervision, or preprocessing rather than the specific CW formulation. Compute, parameter count, and training budget comparisons are not sufficiently controlled.

The paper claims mitigation of distribution shift, but this is mainly inferred from qualitative plots and performance on standard splits. There is no explicit distribution-shift benchmark, controlled shifted test set, or comparison to strong shift-handling methods such as normalization/adaptation approaches.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement says 'The code is available at:' but no repository or artifact is provided in the manuscript. Many implementation details for the base models and hyperparameter tuning protocol are deferred or only partially specified.

Some metric definitions and descriptions appear problematic. For example, the stated correlation score normalizes covariance by products of variances rather than standard deviations, which would not be a standard correlation coefficient unless this is a notation error. The ProbMSE/ProbMAE text also seems inconsistent with the displayed formula using the sample mean.

The experimental scope is narrower than the broad claims suggest: all main tasks use fixed long-horizon forecasting settings, mostly standard datasets, and no comparison to strong non-generative probabilistic forecasters or calibration-focused baselines.

Several results show exceptions or tradeoffs that are under-discussed, e.g. degradation on some QICE/CRPS/point metrics and Solar Energy point-forecast results. The win-rate summaries can obscure these cases and do not account for statistical significance across overlapping standard deviations.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting with non-stationarity, heteroscedasticity, and inter-variable dependence.
The core idea of using conditional mean/covariance estimates to whiten the forecasting target is simple, modular, and potentially useful across diffusion and flow-matching models.

The empirical section is reasonably broad in quantity, covering five public datasets, six generative model backbones, multiple probabilistic metrics, repeated runs, and several ablations on the JMCE estimator.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claims are weakly connected to the actual method. The KL analysis concerns closeness to a Gaussian terminal distribution under sufficient conditions, but does not convincingly establish improved sample quality for learned finite-step diffusion/flow models, and the condition is generally unverifiable in practice.

There is a mismatch between the theory and implementation: the theory is stated for the true conditional covariance, while the method estimates a sliding-window covariance proxy. The paper does not adequately justify why the theoretical guarantees transfer to this proxy.

Novelty is limited. Much of the method resembles learned conditional centering/scaling/whitening before generative modeling, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from prior-informed diffusion, normalization, and covariance-conditioning approaches.

The experimental evidence is not strong enough for the claims. The paper mainly compares each raw model against its CW version, rather than demonstrating that the proposed method is competitive against the best existing forecasting methods in absolute terms. Several CW variants still underperform stronger raw baselines, and the win-rate framing obscures this.

The distribution-shift claim is not convincingly evaluated. It is mostly inferred from qualitative plots and standard train/test splits, without controlled shift benchmarks, shift severity analysis, or comparison to methods designed for distribution shift such as normalization/adaptation baselines.

Evaluation details raise concerns. Conditional FID depends on a TS2Vec representation whose training protocol is unclear, some reported variances are large, statistical significance is not tested, and several improvements appear small or inconsistent across metrics.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the reproducibility statement says code is available but provides no actual link, and many implementation details for integrating CW into the six backbones are deferred or underspecified.

The paper has clarity and polish issues, including typos, notation overload, formatting problems, and occasional citation/reference inconsistencies, which make the technical contribution harder to assess.

strengths: Clear and useful idea: conditioning generative time-series forecasters on learned conditional mean and covariance via whitening is simple, modular, and well motivated for non-stationarity, heteroscedasticity, and inter-variable dependence.

Broad empirical evaluation across five real-world datasets and six generative backbones shows mostly consistent improvements, especially for ProbCorr and Conditional FID, with repeated runs and reported standard deviations.
The framework is presented for both diffusion and flow matching, making the contribution more general than a single-model modification.
The paper includes meaningful ablations on covariance vs variance vs mean priors, eigenvalue regularization, sliding-window length, JMCE backbones, and computational cost.
Theoretical analysis gives a useful sufficient-condition perspective explaining when learned mean/covariance priors can improve the terminal-distribution KL relative to standard Gaussian noise.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are only loosely connected to the practical method: they concern KL to an ideal terminal Gaussian and sufficient conditions involving true conditional covariance, while the implementation estimates sliding-window covariance and uses learned score/flow models whose errors are not analyzed.

Novelty is moderate: the main mechanism is an affine whitening/re-centering transformation using learned conditional moments, and the paper should position more sharply against prior-informed diffusion methods, normalization methods, and conditional Gaussian terminal distributions.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. In particular, the paper claims mitigation of distribution shift, but evaluation is mostly standard train/test forecasting rather than a controlled or explicit distribution-shift benchmark.

Evaluation is extensive but not fully decisive: several ablations are concentrated on ETTh1, statistical significance is not tested despite overlapping standard deviations, and the fairness of using an additional JMCE model and training pipeline versus raw baselines is not fully discussed.

Computational cost is a real limitation for high-dimensional series: Solar Energy requires very large JMCE/whitening time, and the proposed method may be impractical without the accelerated variants, which are not the main evaluated setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the reproducibility statement says code is available but no link is provided, and implementation details may be insufficient to exactly reproduce all baseline integrations.

Some metric definitions and reporting raise concerns, e.g. the correlation formula appears unusual/possibly missing square roots, Conditional FID depends on a learned TS2Vec representation, and the practical meaning of very large FID improvements should be better validated.
